t: Friends Of Appropriate Ages — Counting Valid Requests via Counting Sort
o: Person x sends a request to y (x != y) only if age[y] > 0.5*age[x] + 7, age[y] <= age[x], and NOT (age[y] > 100 && age[x] < 100). Note the third condition is actually redundant: if age[y] > 100 and age[y] <= age[x], then age[x] >= 100 too, so it can never trigger. So the real condition is simply: 0.5*age[x] + 7 < age[y] <= age[x]. In example 1 ([16,16]), each sends to the other since 16 > 15 and 16 <= 16. In example 2, 17->16 and 18->17 are valid but nobody requests an older person. In example 3, only pairs among {100,110,120} with strictly increasing sender age work. Since ages are bounded by 120, we can bucket-count ages instead of comparing all O(n^2) pairs.
k: The condition 'age[y] > 100 && age[x] < 100' is dead code: it can never be true given age[y] <= age[x].
x requests y iff 0.5*age[x] + 7 < age[y] <= age[x]; for a fixed x this defines a contiguous range of ages.
Ages are in [1,120], so counting-sort buckets let us count pairs between age groups instead of iterating over all people.

a.i: Check every ordered pair (x, y) and test the three conditions directly. With n up to 2*10^4 this is ~4*10^8 pair checks, which may TLE in slower languages but is fine conceptually and passes in fast languages. It requires no insight beyond restating the rules.
s: For every ordered pair (i, j) with i != j, evaluate the three conditions.
If none of the conditions blocks the request, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n^2) — all ordered pairs are checked.

a.i: Since ages lie in [1,120], group people by age. For sender age a, valid receiver ages b satisfy 0.5*a + 7 < b <= a. For each pair of ages (a, b), the number of requests is count[a] * count[b], minus count[a] when a == b (no self-requests). Summing over at most 121*121 age pairs gives the answer regardless of n.
s: Build cnt[1..120] where cnt[a] is the number of people aged a.
For each sender age a from 1 to 120, compute lo = floor(a/2) + 7 (smallest invalid b).
For each receiver age b with lo < b <= a, add cnt[a] * cnt[b] to the answer.
If a == b, subtract cnt[a] to exclude self-requests.
a.t: O(n + A^2) where A = 120 — counting is linear, then we check at most 121*121 age pairs.
a.sp: O(A) = O(1) — one fixed-size array of 121 counters.

w: In an interview, state the brute force first, then immediately observe that ages are capped at 120 and pivot to the bucket approach — that observation is the whole problem. Common pitfalls: forgetting to subtract self-pairs when a == b (e.g., [16,16] must return 2, not 4); using strict vs non-strict inequalities incorrectly (b == a is allowed, b == a/2+7 exactly is not); and integer overflow in Java/C++ when multiplying counts (use long). Edge cases: single person returns 0; everyone the same young age like [14,14] returns 0 since 14 <= 14/2+7 = 14. Follow-ups might ask about very large age ranges (then sort + two pointers / prefix sums gives O(n log n)) or streaming input (counting array still works).
